children.author: chank
children.text:
Nobody needs permission to solve an open problem. That's the whole point of publishing them. The question for any result is whether it's correct, not who produced it or whether anyone requested it.

Bringing up OpenAI's lawsuits is irrelevant to whether these proofs hold. And calling a release that includes Lean formalizations a "demonstration of power" gets it backwards. Machine checkable proofs are the least "trust me" form of mathematics there is.

There are fair criticisms here. Not every result is formalized, the model can't be reproduced by outsiders, and the massive dump strains review capacity. Those are reasons to demand full formalization, open access to the methods, and help funding human review. They aren't reasons to dismiss correct mathematics or to tell people to stop working on hard problems.

children.author: Revanche1367
children.text:
This visage of mathematicians among the general public is fairly new I think; it may have existed in some intellectual circles but was not common among regular people. It’s fairly common to read about the lives of mathematicians well into the 19th or even early twentieth century where as children or young adults who excelled at mathematics, their parents or guardians attempted to dissuade them from pursuing mathematics as a career because of the difficulty in obtaining lucrative jobs in mathematics unlike fields like law, engineering, etc. This was the case not only in impoverished countries but in western Europe as well.

Side note: it’s often the case that mathematicians and scientists are perceived only in terms of their research work instead of their personal lives or just other aspects of their lives. How many people on sites like HN or Reddit, would still perceive, for example, Euler the same way if they learned that along with being a genius in mathematics, he was also a religious fundamentalist who was known for annoying his colleagues with his incessant preaching? My point is not to suggest that this takes away from his mathematical work, but it is an indication that the perception people have about at least some of these figures is not based on their reality.

I kind of see their point.

For thousands of years mathematics had this aura of being at the pinnacle of human thought and was one of the things that separated us from other species. People like Euler, Gauss, Euclid, Hilbert, Erdos had this aura about that them that they were on the noblest of pursuits - trying to solve problems that had no immediate practical use, and largely needed focused thinking over extended periods of time with the occasional spark of creativity.

Then comes along AI, a mass extinction event to the entire field. It turns out LLMs can think for longer without stopping, have better recall and working memory. What we're seeing now is a 5000-year old set of institutions facing an existential threat because they no longer require humans to be the sole source of labor.

I find the closest analogy to be automobiles displacing the horse-carriage industry in the early 1900s. Horses couldn't protest and rapidly went out of a job, but horse-carriage owners and that industry certainly did.

children.author: spongebobism
children.text:
There are 2 strong points buried between the snark: that the AI math advisory group, which OpenAI announced working with just 2 1/2 weeks ago, is against using internal models to solve open problems (per their general guidelines[0]); and that this mode of dumping results before having a friendly formulation doesn't center human understanding.

IMO OpenAI's way of publishing also goes against other parts of the general guidelines. Also, I doubt they'll follow point 2B3:

> For each result released, the AI lab should make public the name of the model, the prompts used, a (summarized) chain of thought, the time taken, and the estimated cost of computation. Releasing additional material that sheds light on the scientific process that produced the results, such as the initial LLM outputs before they were cleaned up (as recommended in (1) above), is strongly encouraged.

[0] https://agmai.org/general-sep29/

children.text: While I’ve generally been on the side of mathematicians on this debate and will likely continue to be, saying something like mathematicians didn’t ask for this is off-putting. Nobody owns knowledge, experts of a field cannot in any general sense be said to own that field, and in this case, they don’t even speak for all mathematicians. It’s thoroughly “unmathematical” to declare no mathematicians asked for this when they haven’t inquired exhaustively. A statement like that just gives ammo to the people suggesting that they’re just trying to gatekeep their own field (which IMO may be true at some level for some mathematicians but is not the only reason to be against AI replacing human intellectual pursuits).
